claim: 97% of nodules were infected by either Fix+ or Fix- bacteria in co-inoculation experiments.

claim: A marked difference in the reproductive fitness of Fix+ and Fix- bacteria from the same plant was observed over time, significantly differing from 21 days post-infection.
source: We observed a marked difference in the reproductive fitness of Fix+ and Fix- bacteria from the same plant over time, which significantly differed from 21 days post-infection (dpi) and up to 28 fold on average (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1), perhaps because of plant control mechanisms, including sanctions (Kiers et al., 2003) and possibly PFF.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, with a citation to Kiers et al., 2003 for context on plant control mechanisms.

claim: The reproductive fitness of Fix+ bacteria was up to 28 fold higher on average than Fix- bacteria.
source: We observed a marked difference in the reproductive fitness of Fix+ and Fix- bacteria from the same plant over time, which significantly differed from 21 days post-infection (dpi) and up to 28 fold on average (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1), perhaps because of plant control mechanisms, including sanctions (Kiers et al., 2003) and possibly PFF.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1.

claim: A significant difference in bacterial fitness was obtained from 28 dpi when analyzing control plants singly-infected with either Fix+ or Fix- strains.
source: A significant difference was also obtained from 28 dpi when analyzing control plants singly-infected with either Fix+ or Fix- strains (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Non-fixers did not proliferate better than fixers even at 14 dpi.
source: Non-fixers did not proliferate better than fixers even at 14 dpi (Figure 1A) possibly because the metabolic cost paid by bacteria to fix nitrogen in terms of ATP and reducing power is too low to be detected in our experimental conditions, or because plant sanctions/PFF and the metabolic cost of nitrogen fixation equilibrate until sanctions become prominent.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1A, with speculation about possible reasons.

claim: The metabolic cost paid by bacteria to fix nitrogen in terms of ATP and reducing power may be too low to be detected in the experimental conditions.

claim: The resulting net fitness cost of cooperation appeared to be zero or negative, enabling mutualism to spread.

claim: The differential fitness was not due to a better nodulation competitiveness of Fix+ bacteria.

The number of nodules formed by each strain was indeed proportional to the inoculum ratio (1/1) throughout the time course (Figure 3), confirming that bacterial nitrogen-fixing ability is not selected at the root entry level (Hahn and Studer, 1986; Westhoek et al., 2017).

claim: The control of mutualism acts at the nodule cell scale.
source: In conclusion we provide evidence for differential spatio-temporal dynamics of N2-fixing and non-fixing partners during the symbiotic process, highlighting the importance of considering temporal variations when studying the evolution of cooperative interactions (Barker and Bronstein, 2016). We established that the control of mutualism (i) acts at the nodule cell scale, (ii) occurs relatively early, ca. 16–21 days after inoculation when the wild-type nitrogenase is fully active in Fix+ bacteria (Figure 7) and (iii) leads to up a ca. 80 fold relative increase in mutualistic partners.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental observations from the study.

claim: An increase in frequency of the best cooperators among natural strains was observed after three consecutive nodulation cycles between Medicago truncatula and Sinorhizobium meliloti.
source: It is worth noting that an increase in frequency of the best cooperators among natural strains was also observed after three consecutive nodulation cycles between Medicago truncatula and Sinorhizobium meliloti (Heath and Tiffin, 2009), indicating that the selective advantage of the best N2-fixing strains seems to be robust to the natural diversity of symbiotic associations.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Heath and Tiffin, 2009.

claim: Nitrogen fixation per se determines the in planta spatio-temporal fate of endosymbiotic bacteria.
source: Here we provide conclusive evidence that nitrogen fixation per se, the ultimate trait that turns a parasitic rhizobium-legume association into a mutualistic one, determines the in planta spatio-temporal fate of endosymbiotic bacteria.
evidence: This claim is based on the experimental evidence presented in the study.

source: Non-N2-fixing symbionts do not persist within cells of indeterminate nodules even when they share a nodule with N2-fixing symbionts, indicative of a cell autonomous senescence program as recently shown for determinate nodules (Regus et al., 2017).

claim: Non-N2-fixing symbionts not persisting within cells is indicative of a cell autonomous senescence program.

claim: Control mechanisms prevent social dilemma and help cooperation persist.
source: Since control mechanisms prevent social dilemma –i.e. the possibility that one partner increases its own fitness by decreasing its investment in mutualism- and help cooperation persist (Kiers and Denison, 2008; Frederickson, 2013; Sachs et al., 2004), non-fixers do not threaten mutualism in our system.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kiers and Denison, 2008, Frederickson, 2013, and Sachs et al., 2004.

claim: Non-fixers do not threaten mutualism in the C. taiwanensis-M. pudica system.

claim: Low quality rhizobial partners rarely benefit from low investment in mutualism.
source: Nevertheless, our results provide an additional example supporting the emerging idea that low quality rhizobial partners rarely benefit from low investment in mutualism (Jones et al., 2015; Friesen, 2012).

source: Vertical transmission is expected to promote fitness alignment of obligate symbionts and their partners (Herre et al., 1999).

claim: Horizontal transmission generates more complex ecological cycles for facultative symbionts.
source: In contrast, horizontal transmission generates more complex ecological cycles for facultative symbionts.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: The large number of possible strategies to maximize fitness, and the ability to segregate in a population of genetically variable partners, often entails conflicts of interests between symbionts and their hosts.
source: The large number of possible strategies to maximize fitness, and the ability to segregate in a population of genetically variable partners, often entails conflicts of interests between symbionts and their hosts (Bever et al., 2009; Sachs et al., 2010; Porter and Simms, 2014; Jones et al., 2015) that may result in the classic Tragedy of the Commons (Hardin, 1968).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Bever et al., 2009, Sachs et al., 2010, Porter and Simms, 2014, and Jones et al., 2015.

claim: Conflicts of interests between symbionts and their hosts may result in the classic Tragedy of the Commons.
source: The large number of possible strategies to maximize fitness, and the ability to segregate in a population of genetically variable partners, often entails conflicts of interests between symbionts and their hosts (Bever et al., 2009; Sachs et al., 2010; Porter and Simms, 2014; Jones et al., 2015) that may result in the classic Tragedy of the Commons (Hardin, 1968).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Hardin, 1968.

claim: The emergence and stability of mutualism requires that proliferation of symbionts is allowed but restricted to appropriate spaces and times and that beneficial partners are ultimately favored over uncooperative ones.
source: The emergence and stability of mutualism thus requires that proliferation of symbionts is allowed but restricted to appropriate spaces and times and that beneficial partners are ultimately favored over uncooperative ones (Vigneron et al., 2014; Visick and McFall-Ngai, 2000; Koch et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Vigneron et al., 2014, Visick and McFall-Ngai, 2000, and Koch et al., 2014.

claim: The theoretical aspects of the evolution and maintenance of mutualistic interactions have been extensively discussed.
source: The theoretical aspects of the evolution and maintenance of mutualistic interactions have been extensively discussed (Archetti et al., 2011; Akcay, 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Archetti et al., 2011 and Akcay, 2015.

claim: Experimental assessment of mutualism evolution is scarce.
source: Yet experimental assessment is scarce and the impact of ecological factors, such as population size of hosts and symbionts or the duration of the interaction, has been under-explored, although they are an essential component of the evolutionary potential of symbiotic systems.
evidence: This is based on the authors' assessment of the literature.

claim: The impact of ecological factors, such as population size of hosts and symbionts or the duration of the interaction, has been under-explored.
source: Yet experimental assessment is scarce and the impact of ecological factors, such as population size of hosts and symbionts or the duration of the interaction, has been under-explored, although they are an essential component of the evolutionary potential of symbiotic systems.
evidence: This is based on the authors' assessment of the literature.

claim: Ecological factors are an essential component of the evolutionary potential of symbiotic systems.
source: Yet experimental assessment is scarce and the impact of ecological factors, such as population size of hosts and symbionts or the duration of the interaction, has been under-explored, although they are an essential component of the evolutionary potential of symbiotic systems.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Rhizobia induce the formation of and massively colonize nodules, where intracellular bacteria fix atmospheric nitrogen for the benefit of the plant in exchange for photosynthates.
source: Rhizobia, the N2-fixing symbionts of legumes, induce the formation of and massively colonize nodules, where intracellular bacteria fix atmospheric nitrogen for the benefit of the plant in exchange for photosynthates.
evidence: This is based on established knowledge about rhizobia-legume symbiosis.

claim: When the nodule senesces, nodule bacteria are released to the soil where they can return to free-living lifestyle and/or colonize a new host.
source: When the nodule senesces, nodule bacteria are released to the soil where they can return to free-living lifestyle and/or colonize a new host (Thies et al., 1995).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Thies et al., 1995.

claim: During evolution, symbiosis modules carrying genes essential for the symbiotic process have spread to many different taxa so that extant rhizobia are distributed in hundreds of species in 14 genera of α- and β-proteobacteria.
source: During evolution, symbiosis modules carrying genes essential for the symbiotic process have spread to many different taxa so that extant rhizobia are distributed in hundreds of species in 14 genera of α- and β-proteobacteria (Remigi et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Remigi et al., 2016.

claim: Acquisition of symbiotic genes may not be sufficient to create an effective symbiont and may lead to bacteria exhibiting various levels of symbiotic capacities.
source: Acquisition of symbiotic genes may not be sufficient to create an effective symbiont and may lead to bacteria exhibiting various levels of symbiotic capacities (Nandasena et al., 2006; Nandasena et al., 2007; Marchetti et al., 2010) that can be further optimized and maintained under legume selection pressure (Marchetti et al., 2017; Marchetti et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Nandasena et al., 2006, Nandasena et al., 2007, and Marchetti et al., 2010.

claim: Symbiotic capacities can be further optimized and maintained under legume selection pressure.
source: Acquisition of symbiotic genes may not be sufficient to create an effective symbiont and may lead to bacteria exhibiting various levels of symbiotic capacities (Nandasena et al., 2006; Nandasena et al., 2007; Marchetti et al., 2010) that can be further optimized and maintained under legume selection pressure (Marchetti et al., 2017; Marchetti et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Marchetti et al., 2017 and Marchetti et al., 2014.

claim: Bacteria better able to form and infect nodules are selected by a partner choice mechanism involving the specific recognition of bacterial molecular signals by plant receptors.
source: It has been established that bacteria better able to form and infect nodules are selected by a partner choice mechanism involving the specific recognition of bacterial molecular signals by plant receptors (Kawaharada et al., 2015; Radutoiu et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kawaharada et al., 2015 and Radutoiu et al., 2003.

claim: Bacterial features that are recognized by the plant include Nod factors that initiate rhizobial entry and nodule formation.
source: Bacterial features that are recognized by the plant include Nod factors that initiate rhizobial entry and nodule formation (Perret et al., 2000; Broghammer et al., 2012), and lipo/exopolysaccharides critical for root infection and bacterial release inside the plant cell (Kawaharada et al., 2015), as well as an array of bacterial effectors that refine host specificity (Deakin and Broughton, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Perret et al., 2000 and Broghammer et al., 2012.

claim: Lipo/exopolysaccharides are critical for root infection and bacterial release inside the plant cell.
source: Bacterial features that are recognized by the plant include Nod factors that initiate rhizobial entry and nodule formation (Perret et al., 2000; Broghammer et al., 2012), and lipo/exopolysaccharides critical for root infection and bacterial release inside the plant cell (Kawaharada et al., 2015), as well as an array of bacterial effectors that refine host specificity (Deakin and Broughton, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kawaharada et al., 2015.

claim: An array of bacterial effectors refine host specificity.
source: Bacterial features that are recognized by the plant include Nod factors that initiate rhizobial entry and nodule formation (Perret et al., 2000; Broghammer et al., 2012), and lipo/exopolysaccharides critical for root infection and bacterial release inside the plant cell (Kawaharada et al., 2015), as well as an array of bacterial effectors that refine host specificity (Deakin and Broughton, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Deakin and Broughton, 2009.

claim: Nitrogen fixation is uncoupled from nodulation and infection.
source: Nitrogen fixation however is uncoupled from nodulation and infection, and legumes can be nodulated and infected by ineffective symbiotic partners (Gehlot et al., 2013; Gourion et al., 2015).
evidence: This is based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Legumes can be nodulated and infected by ineffective symbiotic partners.
source: Nitrogen fixation however is uncoupled from nodulation and infection, and legumes can be nodulated and infected by ineffective symbiotic partners (Gehlot et al., 2013; Gourion et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gehlot et al., 2013 and Gourion et al., 2015.

claim: The emergence of mutualism in populations resulting from the transfer of symbiosis modules, and its maintenance over evolutionary timescales indicates that the cooperative behaviour of the bacterial symbionts is controlled at the infection and/or post-infection levels by one or a combination of mechanisms.
source: The emergence of mutualism in populations resulting from the transfer of symbiosis modules, and its maintenance over evolutionary timescales (Werner et al., 2014) indicates that the cooperative behaviour of the bacterial symbionts is controlled at the infection and/or post-infection levels by one or a combination of mechanisms.
evidence: This claim is inferred from the observation of mutualism emergence and maintenance, with a citation to Werner et al., 2014.

claim: Partner choice is the selection of appropriate symbionts at the (pre-) infection stage based on signal recognition.
source: Partner choice is the selection of appropriate symbionts at the (pre-) infection stage based on signal recognition while post-infection sanctions rely on the ability to discriminate between low- and high-quality cooperators during an established interaction and to punish or reward them accordingly (Kiers and Denison, 2008; Frederickson, 2013).
evidence: This is a definition based on established knowledge in the field.

claim: Post-infection sanctions rely on the ability to discriminate between low- and high-quality cooperators during an established interaction and to punish or reward them accordingly.
source: Partner choice is the selection of appropriate symbionts at the (pre-) infection stage based on signal recognition while post-infection sanctions rely on the ability to discriminate between low- and high-quality cooperators during an established interaction and to punish or reward them accordingly (Kiers and Denison, 2008; Frederickson, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kiers and Denison, 2008 and Frederickson, 2013.

claim: Partner-fidelity feedback (PFF) ensures positive assortment of symbionts during long lasting or repeated interactions in spatially structured environments independently from any recognition process or conditional response.
source: Partner-fidelity feedback (PFF) ensures positive assortment of symbionts during long lasting or repeated interactions in spatially structured environments independently from any recognition process or conditional response (Sachs et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sachs et al., 2004.

claim: Different control mechanisms have been proposed to affect the dynamics of mutualistic traits, particularly in the context of the nitrogen-fixing symbiosis.
source: These different control mechanisms have been proposed to affect the dynamics of mutualistic traits, particularly in the context of the nitrogen-fixing symbiosis (Kiers et al., 2003; Oono et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kiers et al., 2003 and Oono et al., 2009.

claim: During the symbiotic process, most rhizobia enter the legume root via infection threads that ensure colonization of the forming nodule and ultimately release bacteria into nodule cells where differentiated forms called bacteroids fix nitrogen.
source: During the symbiotic process, most rhizobia enter the legume root via infection threads that ensure colonization of the forming nodule and ultimately release bacteria into nodule cells where differentiated forms called bacteroids fix nitrogen (Batut et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Batut et al., 2004.

claim: Fix+ and Fix- strains only differed by the presence of the nifH gene, encoding the nitrogenase reductase subunit of the nitrogenase enzyme, and of constitutively expressed GFP or mCherry fluorescent genes.
source: Fix+ and Fix- strains only differed by the presence of the nifH gene, encoding the nitrogenase reductase subunit of the nitrogenase enzyme, and of constitutively expressed GFP or mCherry fluorescent genes.
evidence: This describes the experimental design of the study.

claim: Nodules were only collected from 14 dpi for technical reasons.
source: For technical reasons (see Materials and methods), nodules were only collected from 14 dpi.
evidence: This describes a methodological constraint of the study.

claim: Each nodule was individually analyzed for bacterial fitness by plating, allowing analysis at the nodule and plant individual levels.
source: Importantly, each nodule was individually analyzed for bacterial fitness by plating, allowing analysis at the nodule and plant individual levels.
evidence: This describes the experimental methodology.

claim: Co-infected nodules represented ca. 3% of the nodules when plants were inoculated with 10^6 bacteria/plant.
source: Co-infected nodules represented ca. 3% (A) or 20% (B) of the nodules.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: Co-infected nodules represented ca. 20% of the nodules when plants were inoculated with 10^10 bacteria/plant.
source: Co-infected nodules represented ca. 3% (A) or 20% (B) of the nodules.
evidence: This claim is based on experimental data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The wild-type nitrogenase is fully active in Fix+ bacteria at ca. 16-21 days after inoculation.
source: We established that the control of mutualism (i) acts at the nodule cell scale, (ii) occurs relatively early, ca. 16–21 days after inoculation when the wild-type nitrogenase is fully active in Fix+ bacteria (Figure 7) and (iii) leads to up a ca. 80 fold relative increase in mutualistic partners.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 7.

claim: N2-fixing symbionts progressively outcompete isogenic non-fixers within root nodules, even when they share the same nodule.
source: N2-fixing symbionts progressively outcompete isogenic non-fixers within root nodules, where N2-fixation occurs, even when they share the same nodule.
evidence: This is a summary claim from the abstract, supported by the experimental data in the manuscript.

claim: Rare fixers will invade a population dominated by non-fixing bacteria during serial nodulation cycles with a probability that is function of initial inoculum, plant population size and nodulation cycle length.
source: Numerical simulations, supported by experimental validation, predict that rare fixers will invade a population dominated by non-fixing bacteria during serial nodulation cycles with a probability that is function of initial inoculum, plant population size and nodulation cycle length.
evidence: This is a summary claim from the abstract, supported by the simulation and experimental data in the manuscript.
